title_en: On the Resurrection of the Dead
author: John Chrysostom
occasion: Chrysostom announces a shift from previous doctrinal discussion to a more ethical and doctrinal treatment of the resurrection, aiming to correct doctrine, order moral life, and answer complaints against God's providence. He develops this through sustained exposition of Paul's words in 2 Corinthians.
argument: Belief in the resurrection shapes both doctrine and moral life: it consoles the righteous who suffer and warns the wicked who prosper. Paul repeatedly taught the resurrection to strengthen early Christians under persecution, showing that present affliction already renews the inner person and prepares an eternal weight of glory. Chrysostom explains Paul's image of the earthly tent and heavenly dwelling to argue that the body itself is good, while only corruption and death are destroyed. He defends the body's dignity and the possibility of resurrection from nature and God's creative power, and then presents the gift of the Spirit as a pledge of the resurrection. The homily closes by urging a life worthy of these doctrines.

outline.move: Introduces the theme: belief in the resurrection corrects doctrine, orders life, and answers complaints against God's providence.
Explains present life as a contest and future life as the prize, warning against envying the prosperous wicked.
Describes the many struggles of early Christians: external persecution, internal scandals, and the demanding moral path.
Shows why Paul repeatedly taught the resurrection, citing his own sufferings and his solidarity with believers.
Uses analogies from athletics, seafaring, and Paul's own endurance to argue that present suffering already yields reward before the final prize.
Develops how Paul exemplifies the renewal of the inner person through suffering, quoting Romans and 2 Corinthians, with the soldier image as one supporting analogy.
Contrasts present, visible, temporary troubles with future, invisible, eternal glory, using merchant and farmer analogies.
Argues that worldly laborers trust unseen rewards, so believers should trust God's certain reward even more.
Begins detailed exposition of Paul's words about the earthly tent and the heavenly dwelling.
Explains that we do not wish to be unclothed of the body but to put off corruption and put on immortality, answering those who malign the body.
Defends the body's goodness and dignity, and argues from seeds and metals that corruption precedes renewal.
Argues from God's original creation of the body and from the universal resurrection that God can raise the dead.
Explains that all will rise, but the wicked will rise to punishment; God's purpose from the beginning was immortality, shown in Abel, Enoch, and Elijah.
Points to the Spirit's present gifts, especially baptism and the mysteries, as a pledge of the resurrection, and exhorts to a worthy life.

cast.name: Christ

cast.who: the Creator and Father who will raise the dead.

cast.who: the first righteous man, cited in section 13 as proof of a future reward.

cast.who: quoted in section 8 as speaking of fleeting worldly goods.

scripture: Chrysostom quotes the Greek Old Testament and the Pauline epistles. He cites 2 Corinthians extensively, especially 4:7–5:5, and also Romans 8:35–37, Hebrews 10:32–34, Galatians 3:4, and 1 Corinthians 15. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and LXX Psalm numbering where applicable.
uncertain: The precise date and place of delivery are not stated in the text.
The exact identity of the congregation is not given.
Whether the homily was delivered as part of a continuous series on 2 Corinthians is not explicit in the source.
